title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate for Window cleaning (all heights)
audience: Owners and crew leads in window cleaning who quote residential and small commercial glass work, including solo operators.
learningOutcomes: Write a window cleaning offer with a clear result, time frame, conditions and fix-first promise
Identify the friction and risk the customer carries, such as access, height and streaks, and reduce them
Price a window package on value, storey and access, then check it against your own hours

instruction.heading: What a window customer buys
instruction.body: A window customer buys a clean result inside and out, and the certainty that a missed pane will be put right. 'I will clean your windows' describes a task. 'I will clean every pane in the quote, check each one in daylight before I leave, and come back within a time I have checked against my own records for any pane that fails' describes an offer. The return-visit promise must be one you can keep, so set it from your own return record.

instruction.heading: The five parts of a window offer
instruction.body: State the outcome (every pane in the quote clean on both sides, with frames and sills wiped). State the time frame from past jobs you have timed. List what the customer must do, such as clearing sills, moving pot plants and opening the gate. Add one certainty element, such as a photo per storey or a sign-off checklist. Name the risk you carry, which is the return visit. Put the scope and exclusions in writing, because a written quote can become binding once it is accepted. Second-storey access that the client has not confirmed belongs on the exclusions list.

instruction.heading: Packages that step up, and what the price evidence can bear
instruction.body: Use three tiers a customer can see: exterior panes only; interior and exterior; interior, exterior and tracks. Stepped packages are one way to present an offer (Jobber Academy, May 2021, updated 8 October 2024), but its examples are lawn care, house cleaning, car detailing and gutter cleaning, not window cleaning. The window price evidence is lead-generation estimates, so read it as a reference band, not an average. What's The Damage gives a Melbourne typical of about $12 per exterior window, $19 for interior and exterior, and $6 per track, with ranges of $6 to $19, $10 to $32 and $3 to $16. Oneflare, a marketplace, gives $8 to $15 per standard pane with no measured basis. Build your tiers from your own hours, as set out in the window BP-05 lesson. Test the order in which you show the tiers: an AI-assistant study found that reversing the order raised take-up of the top plan, but it was not a trade study.

instruction.heading: Storey and access are visible lines
instruction.body: Marketplace listings put a second-storey surcharge at 15 to 30 per cent, limited access at 20 to 40 per cent, and a scheduled-maintenance discount at 10 to 20 per cent (Oneflare, retrieved 9 November 2026, no date shown). These are marketplace claims, not measured rates, so do not copy them. The lead-generation guide uses a separate double-storey band instead: $315 to $680, with a typical of $420, for a double-storey or hard-to-reach property. Show the storey or access line on the quote, with the reason for it.

instruction.heading: One total, with GST stated
instruction.body: Show the all-in total for each package and say whether GST is included. The ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited (last modified 15 July 2026). Western Australia's consumer agency asks for the same disclosure, but that guidance applies to WA quotes.

instruction.heading: Guarantees and the fix-first promise
instruction.body: Services carry consumer guarantees: the work must be done with due care and skill. Consumer Victoria says a business should be given a reasonable chance to fix a minor fault free of charge. The page does not set a fix window, so set one you can keep. A written warranty is optional and sits on top of the statutory rights, and a 'no refunds' line does not override a customer's rights for services (business.gov.au, 27 May 2025). Do not promise that streaks or water marks will never return. No source in this research gives a return interval for window cleaning.

instruction.heading: Height is part of the offer
instruction.body: Work above ground changes the price and the method. The Commonwealth falls code (registered 2016) says ladders are for access, and that an elevating work platform or scaffold should be considered first. That code is not Victorian law. Victoria was not checked for this draft, so before you quote any storey, check the Victorian rule for work at height with WorkSafe Victoria. In NSW, a boom-type platform with a boom of 11 metres or more needs a high-risk work licence (SafeWork NSW, cover dated August 2019). Do not promise a height you cannot reach safely.

procedure: Write the outcome in one sentence a customer would repeat, such as every pane in the quote clean on both sides, with frames and sills wiped.
Time three past jobs by storey and count their return visits. Set the time frame and the fix-first window from those records.
List what the customer must do, such as clearing sills, moving pot plants and opening gates, and reduce each step.
Add one certainty element: a photo per storey or a sign-off checklist.
Build three tiers, price each from your own hours and the storey and access lines, then check the totals against the lead-generation band.
Check the access method for each storey against the Victorian rule before the quote is sent.
Show one all-in total for each tier and state whether GST is included.

workedExamples.situation: A Melbourne window cleaner quotes by the hour. Customers say they cannot tell what the price covers, and a two-storey client is comparing the quote with a lower posted quote.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Rewrite the offer as packages and show what the two-storey line covers.
workedExamples.reasoning: Three tiers (exterior only, interior and exterior, and tracks), a storey line and a fix-first promise give the client something to check. The lead-generation Melbourne band for a double-storey or hard-to-reach property runs from $315 to $680, with a typical of $420, so a quote near that typical is in the expected range for that source. A Sydney marketplace quote of $350 inc GST for 15 windows over two storeys, interior and exterior, is undated and not verified, so it prompts the question of what that quote includes; it is not a rate to match. The owner's own hours and access time decide the final figure.

equipmentAndPpe: Package sheet with three tiers and the all-in total
Storey and access price lines, each with its reason
Photo or checklist template for each storey
Fall-prevention and access equipment as the Victorian working-at-height method requires; PPE as listed in {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Quoting per window with no storey or access line
commonErrors.prevention: Show storey and access as separate lines, each with the reason for it.

commonErrors.error: Treating a lead-generation or marketplace figure as the local average
commonErrors.prevention: Use the band as a reference only. The research found a Melbourne typical of $160 for a small home of up to 10 windows, and a marketplace quote of $475 inc GST for 5 to 10 single-storey windows, so the spread is wide.

commonErrors.error: Making a guarantee you cannot afford to honour
commonErrors.prevention: Limit the promise to a return visit you have timed from your own records.

commonErrors.error: Claiming a result you cannot show
commonErrors.prevention: Use only results you have photographed or measured.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business guidance only. This lesson does not grant any licence. Working at height is not settled here: the Commonwealth code (2015) and the NSW code (2019) are not Victorian rules, and the Victorian rule was not checked. Check the Victorian rule for work at height with WorkSafe Victoria before quoting any storey.

NSW only: a boom-type elevating work platform with a boom of 11 metres or more needs a high-risk work licence (SafeWork NSW). No licence for window cleaning was found in this research, so check the rule in each state where you work.
The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited, so the all-in total and GST status belong on every quote.

qualityStandard: Every window quote shows the package contents, storey and access lines, an all-in total and GST status.
Every guarantee offered is one the business can afford and has timed from its own records.
Every storey above ground has a recorded access method, checked against the Victorian rule before the quote is sent.
documentationEvidence: Package sheet with the three tiers and the date it was set
Storey and access line log, with the source of each figure
summary: A window customer buys a clean result and the certainty that a missed pane will be fixed.
Use lead-generation bands as a reference, not an average, and price from your own hours.
Storeys and access are visible lines, and height is checked against the Victorian rule first.

officialReferences.title: Setting prices: what's allowed (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: Taken from the SOL-03 research file (tactic 11); the page was not reopened for this variant. Misleading price statements are prohibited, and an all-in price with GST status is the safer presentation. Publisher: ACCC.

sourceReferences: ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited; all-in price with GST status.

business.gov.au, 'Prepare quotes', https://business.gov.au/people/contractors/prepare-quotes, last updated 1 August 2025. Supports: a written quote can become binding once accepted; scope and exclusions in writing.

business.gov.au, 'Warranties and refunds', https://www.business.gov.au/Products-and-services/Fair-trading/Warranties-and-refunds, last updated 27 May 2025. Supports: an optional warranty sits on top of consumer guarantees; a no-refunds line does not override service rights.

Consumer Victoria, 'Services not done with due care and skill', https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/products-and-services/problem-with-a-service/services-not-done-with-due-care-and-skill, last updated 13 October 2023. Supports: a reasonable chance to fix a minor fault; no fix-window length is given.

Jobber Academy, 'Good, Better, Best Pricing Examples', https://getjobber.com/academy/good-better-best-pricing-examples/, published May 2021, updated 8 October 2024. Older source. Supports: stepped packages.
INSEAD Knowledge, 'Small Change, Big Rewards', https://knowledge.insead.edu/marketing/small-change-big-rewards, 2 October 2025. Non-trade study; first purchase only.

What's The Damage, 'Window cleaning cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/window-cleaning-cost-melbourne/, page verified November 2026, metadata 2026-11-01. Lead-generation guide; estimates, not measured figures.

Oneflare, 'Window cleaner costs', https://oneflare.com.au/costs/window-cleaner, no publication date shown (headline says 2025), retrieved 2026-11-09. Marketplace; surcharges are unmeasured claims; the Sydney quote is undated and unverified.

Work Health and Safety (Managing the Risk of Falls at Workplaces) Code of Practice 2015, https://legislation.gov.au/F2016L00425/asmade/2016-03-30/text/original/epub/OEBPS/document_1/document_1.html, registered 2016, signed 17 December 2015. Commonwealth code; not Victorian law.

SafeWork NSW, 'Managing the risk of falls at workplaces' code, https://www.safework.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/50076/Managing-the-risk-of-falls-at-workplaces-COP.pdf, cover dated August 2019. NSW only.
WA Consumer Protection, 'Estimates, quotes and deposits', https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/estimates-quotes-and-deposits, last updated 4 September 2026. Western Australia only.
Note: Victorian OHS rules were not checked for this draft. Gaps: no strata, real-estate or gutter client evidence for window cleaning was found.
